In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 3:00 03:00 Elon Musk to give away one SpaceX share to every American child next year Squawk Box Europe SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said Monday that he'll give every child in the U.S. one of his shares in the company next year. Musk currently owns about 4.8 billion SpaceX shares, according to an August SEC filing. That figure rises to 6.4 billion when taking into account unvested awards and stock options, representing a 48.4% beneficial stake in the company. There were 72 million children under 18 in the U.S. as of July 1, 2025, according to official census data. That would amount to the CEO giving away about $10.5 billion worth of shares, taking into account SpaceX's closing stock price of $146.03 as of Friday. "This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post on X, without providing further details on how the share giveaway would happen. CNBC has reached out to SpaceX and Musk's family office for further details. Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner, founder of Invest America and Trump Accounts, praised the move and suggested in a post on X that the SpaceX shares could be distributed via Trump accounts. "Incredible Elon!" he wrote. "This will be the largest philanthropic gift in history! 70 M accounts - every citizen under 18 & every child born forevermore now has a free, lifetime investment acct making them an owner in the upside of America & our greatest companies!" Musk's financial giving has been in the news in recent weeks primarily for his political contributions. The Tesla CEO has spent more than $276 million in donations to Republican groups since July, making him the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterm election. The world's richest person poured $158 million into the Senate Leadership Fund, the Republican Party's leading Senate super PAC, in September through an affiliated Texas PAC created to support Republican Ken Paxton. Musk's two contributions of $75 million and $83 million are among the largest political donations ever. Read more CNBC tech news Google says it can build data centers the right way. Some experts and residents are skeptical Women may be at greater risk of AI job losses. Telephone switch operators and PCs show why Anthropic commits 5% of shares to new public benefit fund that could address AI job disruption Always on, always listening: New AI devices are pushing legal limits and could put users in jeopardy When it comes to fulfilling his philanthropic promises , Musk has a spotty track record. For example, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO contributed about $38 million to OpenAI , which he co-founded as a nonprofit research lab, between 2016 and 2020. But he had promised to contribute up to $1 billion, and cut off donations to the organization amid a battle with cofounders for control of the company. In 2021, Musk said he would donate $6 billion to the United Nations World Food Program if it could show him a plan for how they'd use the money to "solve world hunger." While the WFP posted a plan , Musk did not donate. Musk's foundation has also repeatedly fallen shy of making the minimum donations it's required to by law, and as The New York Times previously reported, its donations go to charities that closely benefit Musk and his companies directly. Musk's post came just after Anthropic revealed plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows. In response to an Anthropic post on X about the fund on Sunday, Musk replied, "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," and added that's what he'd be doing. Subject to shareholder approval, Anthropic's fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed. The fund may be used to "explore large donations," including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations, or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said. — CNBC's Jennifer Liu contributed to this report. watch now VIDEO 3:48 03:48 Tesla unveils its next-generation Roadster 'flying car' Squawk Box Europe Choose CNBC as your preferred source on Google and never miss a moment from the most trusted name in business news.

headlines.title: Credit stress is threatening to unwind the AI bull. All eyes are on Oracle to hold the line
headlines.summary: Investors are pushing up the cost of insurance against an Oracle default.
headlines.article_text: oracle-credit-default-swaps-ai-debt Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points AI names like CoreWeave and Oracle were both hit on Friday. Unlike CoreWeave, Oracle is an investment-grade name. However, investors are pushing up the cost of insurance against an Oracle default. In this article ORCL CRWV Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The New York Stock Exchange welcomes executives and guests of Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) to the podium on Sept. 9th, 2026. NYSE Oracle bonds are sitting dangerously close to junk territory as markets cool on artificial intelligence. Much of the AI trade fizzled last week, led by CoreWeave — the neocloud company whose equity and debt has been tanking . Oracle now faces risk of credit rating downgrades that could tip its debt into junk territory — with potentially cascading effects across the AI financing ecosystem. "There seems to be a sentiment shift, which almost speaks to 2026 in general, where we're so bullish about everything and then we're so bearish about everything," said Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners. "It just shows you how quickly this market moves." But there are key differences between CoreWeave and Oracle — the latter is investment grade while Coreweave is already in junk territory. Some analysts and fixed income investors tell CNBC they aren't concerned yet about Oracle and the other hyperscalers. Oracle year to date Still, the shift in sentiment can be seen in the spread of Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The range is more in line with BB and B credit, which is high yield, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence. The spread on Oracle's five-year CDS is currently 295 basis points, after briefly hitting 300 bps on Thursday, up 287% in one year. "Oracle CDS is supported by high liquidity. Nonetheless, its spreads whipsawed over the last few days, no doubt a reflection of the fragile sentiment in AI-related names, notably those in HY [high yield] and at the weaker end of the IG [investment-grade] spectrum, such as Oracle," he said in an email to CNBC. Oracle's 5-year credit default swaps Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CDS means investors view the debt as riskier. Oracle's rating is S&P Credit Ratings is BBB-, the lowest level in the investment-grade spectrum. The agency downgraded Oracle in July, noting that the company's rapidly expanding infrastructure business is increasing its overall credit risk. S&P also said it expects weaker operating cash flow in 2027. A 'bellwether' Oracle is primarily an enterprise software company but it's barreling into data centers and cloud services, including a massive $300 billion deal with OpenAI. To fund the buildout, Oracle has issued $118 billion in long-term debt and has another $39 billion in capital and lease obligations, according to FactSet data. The spending and debt obligations are taking a toll on Oracle's finances while the company waits for a gusher of AI revenue. Analysts estimate free cash flow of -$23.7 billion this year and -$36 billion in 2027, according to consensus forecasts. That would be bad enough for investors, but Oracle is more than just a debt-laden data center play. It's become an AI "bellwether," notes Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research at Deutsche Bank. A downgrade of its credit into junk territory "would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," he said in a report. S&P said in its July downgrade that another downgrade could be triggered by: an expectation that Oracle will sustain leverage exceeding 4x; or belief that the software company isn't on a path to generate positive free operating cash flow by fiscal 2029; or a negative view on Oracle's AI strategy or that of the overall AI industry. As an investment-grade company, Oracle can borrow cheaply and with duration, but that would change with a junk rating, said Jamie Meyers, a senior securities analyst at Laffer Tengler, which owns Oracle stock. "Nobody in high yield is going to buy a 30 year debt," he said. "Getting downgraded to junk would mean that they'd have to push everything short. Obviously, their borrowing rate would be higher, more than likely." That said, Meyers is not concerned about Oracle's debt levels. In a meeting between Oracle and Laffer Tengler last year, Oracle stressed it will defend its investment-grade rating, Meyers said. "We do believe the revenue is going to start ramping and the earnings are going to start ramping," he said. "What Oracle really needs is … time. They need to get these things built." Brad Collins, a fixed income portfolio manager at Vanguard, also expressed confidence in Oracle and the other hyperscalers. "Oracle is most under the microscope, but as a result, has been more diligent in their issuance" so far this year, he said. "Balance sheets are in a healthy starting spot, and [I] would not extrapolate what we are seeing in HY to IG." The company's current troubles could be looked at as a "financing test," said Dynasty Financial Partners' Nerney. They'll either pass or fail, which could mean an additional downgrade, he said. "The real question now is, with the move in rates, how much is that going to cost?" he said. "If rates continue to move higher, just the opportunity cost of investors to hold Oracle paper relative to other things in the market, you're going to see the market demand more." Oracle responded to a request for comment by saying, "We have been very clear that maintaining an investment grade rating is our first priority as a company." "The AI infrastructure business has strong economic returns and we expect it will produce strong free cash flows once projects are ramped," it added.
